'''Margaret Hope Alston-Garnjost''' (also published as Margaret Alston, January 23, 1929 – February 7, 2019) was a British physicist who worked for many years at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], where her research with the [[bubble chamber]] contributed to the [[Nobel Prize]] winning work of her supervisor [[Luis Walter Alvarez]].{{r|chron|liver}}

==Education and career==
Alston-Garnjost was born in London on January 23, 1929; her parents were Pauline and Norman Alston.{{r|liver}} To escape [[World War II]], her parents sent her to be schooled at [[St. Cyprian's School, Cape Town]] in [[South Africa]], living with cousins in Cape Town.{{r|chron}} She completed a Ph.D. in physics at the [[University of Liverpool]] in 1955.{{r|liver}}

After completing her Ph.D., she took a position at the [[Lawrence Radiation Laboratory]] in [[Berkeley, California]], which eventually became the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]]. There, she met and married fellow laboratory employee Bertram Garnjost in 1966.{{r|liver|chron}} Her supervisor, [[Luis Walter Alvarez]], earned the Nobel Prize for his work with the [[bubble chamber]] in 1968, and he noted Alston's work in his acceptance speech, joking based on the similarity in their names that their publications were by "Alston et al".{{r|chron}} Her later work also included experiments on [[double beta decay]] with Robert Kenney and Robert D. Tripp, conducted in an abandoned mine in [[Idaho]].{{r|idaho}}

After retiring, Alston-Garnjost and her husband moved to Oregon, returning to the [[East Bay]] region of California in 2008. She died on February 7, 2019.{{r|chron}}

==Recognition==
Alston-Garnjost was named a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] (APS) in 1984, after a nomination from the APS Division of Nuclear Physics, "for contributions to the discovery and measurements of properties of both light and heavy quark resonances".{{r|faps}}
